To cause moisture to be completely removed from; to make dry.

examples.text: Placing socks on the radiator will dry them out more quickly.

glosses: To have excess water evaporate or be otherwise removed; to become dry.

examples.text: Your trousers need to dry out before you put them on.

glosses: To (cause to) sober up; to cease to be drunk; to quit using drugs or alcohol.
To become less oily, affecting play, after being oiled up.
To become dry (often of weather); to lose water.

examples.text: I'll go shopping when it dries up.
Last summer the lake completely dried up.

But those newcomers need water — water that is vanishing as a megadrought dries up reservoirs and rivers across the West. […] Groundwater and streams vital both to farmers and cities are drying up. […] Gov. Spencer Cox of Utah said all but one of the fields on his family’s farm had dried up.

glosses: To cause to become dry.

examples.text: The heatwave dried up all the rivers.

glosses: To manually dry dishes and utensils.

examples.text: I'll dry up if you wash up.

glosses: To deprive someone of (something vital).

examples.text: The bankruptcy rumor dried up his sales.

glosses: To gradually decrease and eventually cease.

examples.text: When our money dried up, we had to get proper jobs.
After the stock market crash, the easy financing dried up.
This love has dried up and stayed behind

glosses: To stop talking because one has forgotten what one was going to say.

examples.text: This surprised me so much that I dried up for a moment.

To forget one's lines.
To stop talking or drop a topic.

examples.text: Oh, dry up, you old fuddy-duddy!
"Oh, dry up,' said Arnold morosely.

glosses: Secar (uso pronominal de ...).
To shrivel, droop or dry up, especially from lack of water.

examples.text: The flowers began to wither in the hot sun without enough water.
She watched as the old tree slowly withered with time.
Without care, the crops will wither and fail to grow.

glosses: To cause to shrivel or dry up.

examples.text: There was a man which had his hand withered.
This is man, old, wrinkled, faded, withered.

glosses: To lose vigour or power; to languish; to pass away.

examples.text: names that must not wither
States thrive or wither as moons wax and wane.

glosses: To become helpless due to emotion.
To make helpless due to emotion.
singular of withers (“part of the back of a four-legged animal that is between the shoulder blades”)

examples.text: Timozel had slid his feet quickly from the stirrups and swung his leg over the horse's wither as it slumped to the ground, standing himself in one graceful movement.

If a saddle tips too far forward it may rest on the horse's wither and cause pain. There should always be a gap of roughly 5 cm between the horse's wither and the pommel when you are sitting on the saddle.

glosses: Against, in opposition to.
To go against, resist; oppose.
To lose energy or become weak and feeble.

examples.text: She watched him waste away from lack of food or exercise.
The perennial Arctic ice cap—the sea ice that persists through winter and summer—is wasting away. Over the past half century it has shrunk by more than a million square miles

glosses: To lose strength, become weaker; to wane; to disappear or reduce slowly.

examples.text: I was angry at first, but my rage faded away over time.
The stars shall fade away.

"I felt my strength fading away, and I was in a half swoon. How long this horrible thing lasted I know not, but it seemed that a long time must have passed before he took his foul, awful, sneering mouth away. I saw it drip with the fresh blood!"

The sun is fading away
That's the end of the day

glosses: A painting technique in which young women's clothes fade into the background.

examples.text: Hirschfeld captured many scenes in line and employed Coles Phillips's "fade away" technique in his painting on the left.
In Phillip's "Fade Away" style, he is literally editing out elements (by making them the same flat color as the background), but those elements are still there.
Phillips became known for the "fade away, in which the main figures' clothing is the same color as the background, allowing the elements to partially blend.
